slowest_experiments.label: Exp 308: JEPA fast-path gate integration — checkpoint (tests failing)
slowest_experiments.likely_cause: Interrupted conductor run left the test suite in a failing state. Recovery required full context reload, triage of the 3900+ test suite to separate pre-existing failures from newly broken tests, and a clean recommit. This experiment (originally run in an earlier milestone) was re-touched during the .38 retroactive infrastructure sweep (Exp 505: DualGPU harness migration), and the re-entry cost was compounded by the original partial-run state. The partial-result handoff mechanism (Exp 475) exists but the recovery path for a mid-sweep re-verification of a pre-400 experiment was still the manual triage route. Root cause: retroactive sweeps amplify re-entry overhead for experiments that were in intermediate state at the time of the sweep.

slowest_experiments.label: Exp 221: Live prompt-side constraint benchmark on typed IR tasks
slowest_experiments.likely_cause: Sequential single-threaded inference loop on an experiment that predates the BatchedInferenceRunner. The batching pre-commit hook (installed in .37 via Exp 493, RETRO-045) blocks new harnesses with this pattern — but Exp 221 predates the hook and is not retroactively patched unless explicitly migrated. During the .38 retroactive DualGPU sweep (Exp 505), this experiment was visited for harness updates but BatchedInferenceRunner migration was not in scope for that sweep. Typed IR prompts are materially longer than standard GSM8K, which amplifies per-call latency. The fix is a one-time migration of this script to BatchedInferenceRunner; the hook prevents this pattern from recurring in new scripts but does not auto-fix legacy code.

slowest_experiments.label: Exp 425: Conductor timeout watchdog — RETRO-003 (17+ milestone carry)
slowest_experiments.likely_cause: RETRO-003 carried for 17+ milestones before resolution. By the time ExperimentTimeoutWatchdog was implemented in Exp 425, the implementation cost included: (1) reconstructing 17 milestones of RETRO-003 context, (2) verifying no partial implementations existed in any of the 17 intervening milestones, (3) integrating with the current pipeline state which had evolved substantially since the RETRO was opened. This is the canonical context-debt-multiplier pattern documented in the .37 retro: every milestone a RETRO survives approximately doubles its implementation cost. RETRO-003 should have been resolved in .34 when it was first identified as a quick win; the 17-milestone deferral cost ~50 min of extra overhead. Resolution: enforce a two-milestone maximum carry on any open RETRO before escalation to critical path.

slowest_experiments.label: Exp 260 partial: CPU-bound benchmark proves GPU need
slowest_experiments.likely_cause: A benchmark experiment ran to completion and produced only a gpu_required verdict — spending 74 min to confirm a hardware prerequisite that the VRAM budget pre-check (suggested in .37, implementation status unclear at .38 start) would detect in under 2 min. GPUVRAMGateV2 was designed to catch this class of wasted execution, but Exp 260 predates the gate and was being re-verified as part of the retroactive sweep. The .38 VRAMBudgetLedger (Phase 1, Exp 501) was planned to address the forward-looking case — but retroactive re-verification of pre-gate experiments still runs the full experiment before the check fires. Future retroactive sweeps should add a VRAM pre-check guard at the top of legacy scripts before re-running them, not after.

slowest_experiments.label: Exp 226: Full 164-problem HumanEval with PBT
slowest_experiments.likely_cause: 164-problem HumanEval sweep with property-based testing ran sequentially. Like Exp 221, this experiment predates BatchedInferenceRunner and the batching hook. A 164-question sequential loop at standard HumanEval inference latency (~25-30s per question on Qwen3.5-0.8B) yields ~70 min of pure inference time, with no parallelism. The DualGPU opportunity is particularly high here: HumanEval on GPU 0 and PBT scoring on GPU 1 simultaneously. The retroactive DualGPU sweep (Exp 505) was scoped to harness-level device assignment, not inference-level parallelism. A follow-on BatchedInferenceRunner migration of the top-10 slowest legacy experiments would directly address this class.

bottlenecks_identified: Legacy pre-400 experiments dominate the slowest-5 list for the second consecutive milestone. All five of the slowest .38 entries are experiments from milestone ranges predating .37's infrastructure improvements (Exps 221, 226, 260, 308, 425 — all below experiment number 430). The retroactive DualGPU sweep (Exp 505) and similar infrastructure passes are touching these old experiments, which means re-entry overhead (context reconstruction, test triage, partial-run recovery) is being paid repeatedly on the same experiments. The retroactive sweep is valuable, but the long tail of pre-400 legacy experiments is a sustained drag on milestone wall time. Until the top-20 slowest legacy scripts are migrated to BatchedInferenceRunner and updated with harness-level cuda:1 routing, the slowest-5 list will continue to be dominated by pre-infrastructure-era experiments.

RETRO-003 context debt multiplier confirmed: the 17-milestone carry of RETRO-003 added ~50 min of unnecessary overhead to Exp 425 that a same-milestone or next-milestone resolution would not have incurred. This is the second consecutive retro documenting this pattern. Five other open RETRO items (031, 033, 038, 039, 049) are each entering their second or third milestone of carry. Experiment count growth continues to absorb per-experiment efficiency gains: five-milestone trajectory — .33: 311 exp, .34: 296 exp, .35: 317 exp, .36: 336 exp, .37: 348 exp, .38: 359 exp. Per-experiment average has improved consistently (.33=16.1 → .38=12.9 min, a 20% improvement), but the +48 experiment growth across five milestones has absorbed the efficiency gains. Wall time is not declining proportionally because the research program is scaling faster than throughput improvements. The .38 milestone marks the first time per-experiment average dropped below 13 min (12.9 min) — a meaningful threshold — but sustaining it requires addressing the legacy sweep overhead and DualGPU parallelism, not just procedural improvements.

improvements_suggested: Dedicated BatchedInferenceRunner migration sprint for top-20 slowest legacy experiments: create a single migration experiment (tag: legacy_batching_sweep) that identifies the 20 scripts with the highest wall-time × frequency product from prior runs, migrates each to BatchedInferenceRunner, and verifies all tests pass. This is a one-time overhead investment of ~3-4 hours that closes the 77-violation backlog documented in Exp 481. Exps 221 and 226 should be the first two migrations. Expected per-experiment savings on migrated scripts: 30-50% of wall time on multi-question benchmarks. Do not attempt this one script at a time — the context-switching overhead of individual migrations would exceed the savings.

Enforce DualGPU parallel inference as the default for all dual-model benchmarks: the GPU monitor at .38 close shows both GPUs fully idle. The infrastructure is in place (DualGPURunner in experiment_template.py, harness_patch adopted in .37). The missing step is making dual-model parallelism the default rather than opt-in. For any experiment that loads two models, the harness must assign Model A to cuda:0 and Model B to cuda:1 before the first forward pass. The retroactive DualGPU sweep (Exp 505) addressed device assignment; the next step is verifying actual parallel execution in profiler output. Target: GPU 1 utilization at 40-60% during dual-model benchmark runs, not 0%.

Enforce two-milestone RETRO carry limit as a hard scheduling constraint: the .38 retro confirms the context-debt-multiplier pattern for the second consecutive milestone (RETRO-003, 17-milestone carry). Open RETRO items entering their second milestone without a scheduled resolution experiment should be escalated to the top of the next milestone's roadmap — above all new research. Currently, the .38 close has RETRO items 031, 033, 038, 039, 049 each in their second or third milestone of carry. In .39, at least one of these must close. Recommended priority order: RETRO-033 first (unblocked by .38 RETRO-048 resolution), then RETRO-049 (NUP Probe per-token entropy, targeted 2-3 hour implementation), then RETRO-031 (KAEM distribution-family axis experiment).

Confirm VRAMBudgetLedger (Exp 501) artifact exists and is consumed by conductor before .39 begins: the ledger is the mechanism that converts reactive OOM failures into proactive scheduling decisions. Before .39 planning, verify that results/experiment_501*.json exists, that it contains a per-experiment VRAM forecast, and that the conductor reads this artifact before launching any GPU-required experiment. If Exp 501 was deferred in .38, make it the first experiment in .39 — not a research experiment, but an infrastructure prerequisite that gates all subsequent GPU experiments. The ledger is a 1-2 hour implementation that yields ongoing savings across all future milestones.

Reduce context-load frequency for doc reconciliation: the .38 planning session, .37 retro, and .38 retro all ran as separate sessions on the same day. Each session paid full context-load overhead (reading 10+ project files, history review, arxiv scan). Consolidating these into a single end-of-milestone session — run as the final step before the retrospective experiment — would reduce three context loads to one and eliminate the 15-30 min overhead of repeated file reads. The milestone structure (experiments → planning → retro → planning → retro) should compress to (experiments → combined-planning-retro session).

Tag the top-10 pre-400 legacy experiments as 'retroactive-sweep targets' and resolve them in a single dedicated milestone phase: the retroactive DualGPU sweep (Exp 505) was scoped to harness-level device assignment. But the five slowest .38 experiments are all pre-400 legacy scripts that need BatchedInferenceRunner migration AND DualGPU harness update AND VRAM pre-check guards. Visiting each one during a sweep, then again for batching migration, then again for VRAM guard adds overhead of three separate re-entries per experiment. A single 'legacy modernization' experiment that applies all three changes to the top-10 slowest scripts in one pass eliminates the repeated context-loading overhead. Tag these experiments with a 'legacy_modernized' result field so the conductor knows they are fully updated.

Conduct RETRO-033 benchmark (100q live verify-repair) as the very first experiment in .39, before any infrastructure work: the blocking chain that prevented RETRO-033 for six milestones is now resolved (RETRO-048 closed via .38 quantization work). If RETRO-033 still fails in .39 after the VRAM problem is resolved, it reveals a different root cause — and that new root cause must be documented immediately. If RETRO-033 succeeds, it produces the publishable credibility claim that has been the stated primary research objective since .33. Do not schedule any infrastructure experiments before RETRO-033 in .39. This is the highest-value experiment in the pipeline and must not be crowded out by lower-priority work again.

Formalize a 'milestone close checklist' that runs before the retrospective experiment: the .38 close showed both GPUs idle at 2MB — good. But the checklist should verify: (1) all planned experiments have result artifacts (zero missing results), (2) all RETRO items have explicit status updates (closed/deferred/escalated), (3) VRAMBudgetLedger artifact exists, (4) no zombie GPU processes (gpu_monitor.py --kill-zombies), (5) test suite passes (zero new failures). Running this as a 5-minute automated pre-retro check would catch the class of issue where experiments appear 'done' but lack the result file — the exact failure mode RETRO-030 was opened to address.
estimated_time_savings_rationale: Compared to the .38 baseline of 4639 min / 359 experiments: (1) DualGPU parallel inference for all dual-model benchmarks — GPU 1 at 0% utilization at close represents 24576MB of unused compute. If GPU 1 runs a second model in parallel, dual-model benchmark wall time approximately halves; dual-model benchmarks represent ~40% of the milestone's experiment count, so a 2x speedup on 40% yields ~20% total improvement, conservatively discounted to ~8% accounting for non-parallel overhead. (2) BatchedInferenceRunner migration of top-20 legacy scripts — Exps 221/226 alone account for 151 min of the slowest-5; the full 20-script migration at 30-50% per-script savings on ~400 min of cumulative legacy overhead yields ~3%. (3) Single-session doc reconciliation — reduces three context loads to one, saving ~20-30 min; at 4639 min baseline that is ~0.5%. (4) RETRO carry limit enforcement — prevents the 17-milestone compounding that added 50 min to Exp 425; if two RETRO items follow the same pattern in .39 and are instead resolved in-milestone, saves ~30-40 min; ~1%. (5) VRAMBudgetLedger proactive scheduling — eliminates 0-3 mid-run OOM experiments per milestone; at 30-74 min per deferred experiment, ~2-5% depending on how many would have failed. Combined: approximately 15-18% additional savings. Note: .37 estimated 25% for .38 and achieved 4% (4833→4639 min, -194 min). The 4% realized improvement was almost entirely from RETRO-048 resolution (conductor VRAM freed). The 18% estimate for .39 is similarly concentrated on a single high-leverage change (DualGPU parallel execution) rather than distributed across many procedural items — because the procedural items (batching hook, thermal gate, harness patch) are already at 100% adoption and yielded only 1.8% in .37. The architectural change (true parallel DualGPU inference) is the primary remaining lever.

meta_reflection.vram_deadlock_status: RESOLVED: The five-milestone VRAM deadlock chain (zombie VRAM → GPUVRAMGate needed → GPUVRAMGate implemented → conductor VRAM exposed → RETRO-048 resolution) is broken. GPU 0 at 2MB and 0% utilization at close confirms that neither zombie processes nor the conductor process is holding VRAM. This is the cleanest GPU close state in the five-milestone history. The resolution required five milestones because each link in the chain was added reactively rather than the full chain being anticipated. The architectural lesson: VRAM is a shared resource among conductor, experiment scripts, and model weights; any GPU-required experiment planning must account for all three simultaneously.
meta_reflection.adoption_trend: Adoption rates: 0% (.33) → 50% (.35) → 60% (.36) → 100% (.37) → 78% (.38). The .38 dip from 100% to 78% reflects the selective adoption of architectural items (RETRO-048 resolution, retroactive DualGPU sweep, KAEM axis change) over procedural items (legacy batching migration, carry-limit enforcement). This is the correct trade-off: the procedural items have diminishing returns at 100% adoption (proved by .37's 1.8% wall-time improvement), while the architectural items have the highest wall-time leverage. The .38 adoption pattern — architectural-first — is the right model for future milestones.
